metadata.title: Simultaneously Satisfying Linear Equations Over $\mathbb{F}_2$: MaxLin2 and Max-$r$-Lin2 Parameterized Above Average

nodes.name: MaxLin2
nodes.statement: In the problem \textsc{MaxLin2}, we are given a system $S$ consisting of $m$ equations in variables $x_1,\ldots ,x_n$, where each equation is $\prod_{i \in I_j}x_i = b_j$ and $x_i,b_j \in \{-1, 1\}$, $j=1,\ldots ,m$. Equation $j$ is assigned a positive integral weight $w_j$ and we wish to find an assignment of values to the variables in order to maximize the total weight of the satisfied equations.
nodes.statement_short: Maximize the total weight of simultaneously satisfied $\pm 1$ product equations $\prod_{i\in I_j}x_i=b_j$.

nodes.name: Total weight $W$ and ${\rm sat}(S)$
nodes.statement: Let $W$ be the sum of the weights of all equations in $S$ and let ${\rm sat}(S)$ be the maximum total weight of equations that can be satisfied simultaneously.

nodes.name: Tightness of the $W/2$ lower bound on ${\rm sat}(S)$
nodes.statement: To see that $W/2$ is a tight lower bound on ${\rm sat}(S)$ choose assignments to the variables independently and uniformly at random. Then $W/2$ is the expected weight of satisfied equations (as the probability of each equation being satisfied is $1/2$) and thus $W/2$ is a lower bound; to see the tightness consider a system consisting of pairs of equations of the form $\prod_{i\in I}x_i=-1,\ \prod_{i\in I}x_i=1$ of the same weight, for some non-empty sets $I \subseteq [n]$.
nodes.statement_short: A random assignment satisfies weight $W/2$ in expectation, and paired opposite equations show $W/2$ cannot be improved.
assumptions: choose assignments to the variables independently and uniformly at random
conclusions: $W/2$ is the expected weight of satisfied equations
$W/2$ is a lower bound
consider a system consisting of pairs of equations of the form $\prod_{i\in I}x_i=-1,\ \prod_{i\in I}x_i=1$ of the same weight, for some non-empty sets $I \subseteq [n]$

nodes.name: MaxLin2-AA
nodes.origin_citation: H\aa stad 2001; H\aa stad \& Venkatesh 2004; Mahajan, Raman \& Sikdar 2009
nodes.statement: {\sc MaxLin2-AA}\\ \nopagebreak \emph{Instance:} A system $S$ of equations $\prod_{i \in I_j}x_i = b_j$, where $x_i, b_j \in \{-1,1\}$, $j=1,\ldots ,m$; equation $j$ is assigned a positive integral weight $w_j$, and a nonnegative integer $k$.\\ \nopagebreak \emph{Question:} ${\rm sat}(S)\ge W/2 + k$?
nodes.statement_short: Decide whether equations of total weight at least $W/2+k$ can be satisfied simultaneously.

nodes.name: Max-$r$-Lin2-AA
nodes.statement: {\sc Max-$r$-Lin2-AA}\\ \nopagebreak \emph{Instance:} A system $S$ of equations $\prod_{i \in I_j}x_i = b_j$, where $x_i, b_j \in \{-1,1\}$, $|I_j|\le r$, $j=1,\ldots ,m$; equation $j$ is assigned a positive integral weight $w_j$, and a nonnegative integer $k$.\\ \nopagebreak \emph{Question:} ${\rm sat}(S)\ge W/2+k$?
nodes.statement_short: {\sc MaxLin2-AA} restricted to equations with at most $r$ variables each.

nodes.name: H\aa stad's inapproximability of Max-$r$-Lin2-AA
nodes.statement: H\aa stad \cite{Hastad01} proved that, as a maximization problem, {\sc Max-$r$-Lin2-AA} with any fixed $r\ge 3$ (and hence {\sc MaxLin2-AA}) cannot be approximated within $c$ for any $c>1$ unless P$=$NP (that is, the problem is not in APX unless P$=$NP).
nodes.statement_short: For fixed $r\ge 3$, {\sc Max-$r$-Lin2-AA} is not in APX unless P$=$NP.
assumptions: as a maximization problem
{\sc Max-$r$-Lin2-AA} with any fixed $r\ge 3$
conclusions: cannot be approximated within $c$ for any $c>1$ unless P$=$NP

nodes.name: H\aa stad--Venkatesh randomized approximation for Max-$r$-Lin2-AA
nodes.statement: In particular, they proved that for {\sc Max-$r$-Lin2-AA} there exist a constant $c>1$ and a randomized polynomial-time algorithm that, with probability at least 3/4, outputs an assignment with an approximation ratio of at most $c^r\sqrt{m}.$
nodes.statement_short: A randomized polynomial-time algorithm achieves approximation ratio $c^r\sqrt{m}$ with probability $\ge 3/4$.
assumptions: for {\sc Max-$r$-Lin2-AA}
conclusions: there exist a constant $c>1$ and a randomized polynomial-time algorithm that, with probability at least 3/4, outputs an assignment with an approximation ratio of at most $c^r\sqrt{m}.$

nodes.name: Excess and maximum excess
nodes.origin_citation: H\aa stad \& Venkatesh 2004; Crowston, Gutin, Jones, Kim \& Ruzsa 2010
nodes.statement: Define the \emph{excess} for $x^0=(x^0_1,\ldots ,x^0_n)\in \{-1, 1\}^n$ over $S$ to be $$\varepsilon_S(x^0)=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\prod_{i\in I_j}x^0_i,\ \mbox{ where } c_j=w_{j}b_j.$$ Note that $\varepsilon_S(x^0)$ is the total weight of  equations satisfied by $x^0$ minus the total weight of equations falsified by $x^0$. The maximum possible value of $\varepsilon_S(x^0)$ is the {\em maximum excess} of $S$.
nodes.statement_short: The excess of an assignment is satisfied weight minus falsified weight; its maximum over assignments is the maximum excess.
nodes.genus: the total weight of  equations satisfied by $x^0$ minus the total weight of equations falsified by $x^0$

nodes.name: Pseudo-boolean function
nodes.statement: Note that the excess is a {\em pseudo-boolean function} \cite{BorHam2002}, i.e., a function that maps $\{-1,1\}^n$ to the set of reals.
differentia: maps $\{-1,1\}^n$ to the set of reals

nodes.name: Previously known kernels for Max-$r$-Lin2-AA
nodes.origin_citation: Gutin, Kim, Szeider \& Yeo 2011; Crowston et al. 2010; Kim \& Williams 2010
nodes.statement: Gutin et al. \cite{GutKimSzeYeo11} proved that {\sc Max-$r$-Lin2-AA}[$k$] is fixed-parameter tractable and, moreover, has a kernel with $n\le m = O(k^2)$. This kernel is, in fact, a kernel of {\sc Max-$r$-Lin2-AA}[$k,r$] with $n\le m = O(9^rk^2)$. This kernel for {\sc Max-$r$-Lin2-AA}[$k$] was improved by Crowston et al. \cite{CroGutJonKimRuz10}, with respect to the number of variables,  to $n = O(k\log k)$. For {\sc Max-$r$-Lin2-AA}[$k$], Kim and Williams \cite{KimWil} were the first to obtain a kernel with a linear number of variables, i.e., $n = O(k)$. This kernel is, in fact, a kernel with $n\le r(r+1)k$ for  {\sc Max-$r$-Lin2-AA}[$k,r$].
nodes.statement_short: Prior kernels for {\sc Max-$r$-Lin2-AA} went from $O(k^2)$ equations down to $r(r+1)k$ variables.

nodes.name: Unique Fourier expansion of a pseudo-boolean function
nodes.statement: Here we use the following well-known and easy to prove fact \cite{odonn}: each function $f:\ \{-1,1\}^n\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ can be uniquely written as \begin{equation}f(x)=\hat{f}(\emptyset) + \sum_{I\in {\cal F}}\hat{f}(I)\prod_{i\in I}x_i.\end{equation} where ${\cal F}\subseteq \{I:\ \emptyset \neq I\subseteq [n]\}$, $[n]=\{1,2,\ldots ,n\}$ and $\hat{f}(I)$ are non-zero reals.
nodes.statement_short: Every $f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ has a unique multilinear expansion with non-zero coefficients $\hat f(I)$.
assumptions: each function $f:\ \{-1,1\}^n\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$
conclusions: can be uniquely written as \begin{equation}f(x)=\hat{f}(\emptyset) + \sum_{I\in {\cal F}}\hat{f}(I)\prod_{i\in I}x_i.\end{equation}
${\cal F}\subseteq \{I:\ \emptyset \neq I\subseteq [n]\}$, $[n]=\{1,2,\ldots ,n\}$ and $\hat{f}(I)$ are non-zero reals

nodes.name: Fourier expansion, Fourier coefficients and degree of $f$
nodes.statement: Formula (\ref{eq1a}) is the Fourier expansion of $f$ and $\hat{f}(I)$ are the Fourier coefficients of $f$. The right hand size of (\ref{eq1a}) is a polynomial and the degree $\max \{|I|:\ I\in {\cal F}\}$ of this polynomial will be called the {\em degree} of $f$.
differentia: the degree $\max \{|I|:\ I\in {\cal F}\}$ of this polynomial

nodes.name: Parameterized problem
nodes.statement: A \emph{parameterized problem} is a subset $L\subseteq \Sigma^* \times \mathbb{N}$ over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$.

nodes.name: Fixed-parameter tractable (FPT)
nodes.statement: $L$ is \emph{fixed-parameter tractable} (FPT, for short) if the membership of an instance $(x,k)$ in $\Sigma^* \times \mathbb{N}$ can be decided in time $f(k)|x|^{O(1)},$ where $f$ is a function of the parameter $k$ only.
differentia: the membership of an instance $(x,k)$ in $\Sigma^* \times \mathbb{N}$ can be decided in time $f(k)|x|^{O(1)},$ where $f$ is a function of the parameter $k$ only

nodes.name: The class XP
nodes.statement: When the decision time is replaced by the much more powerful $|x|^{O(f(k))},$ we obtain the class XP, where each problem is polynomial-time solvable for any fixed value of $k.$
differentia: the decision time is replaced by the much more powerful $|x|^{O(f(k))},$
each problem is polynomial-time solvable for any fixed value of $k.$

nodes.name: The W-hierarchy tower between FPT and XP
nodes.statement: There is an infinite number of parameterized complexity classes between FPT and XP (for each integer $t\ge 1$, there is a class W[$t$]) and they form the following tower: $FPT \subseteq W[1] \subseteq W[2] \subseteq \cdots \subseteq XP.$ For the definition of the classes W[$t$], see, e.g., \cite{FlumGrohe06}.

nodes.name: Bikernelization, bikernel and its size
nodes.statement: Given a pair $L,L'$ of parameterized problems, a \emph{bikernelization from $L$ to $L'$} is a polynomial-time algorithm that maps an instance $(x,k)$ to an instance $(x',k')$ (the \emph{bikernel}) such that (i)~$(x,k)\in L$ if and only if $(x',k')\in L'$, (ii)~ $k'\leq f(k)$, and (iii)~$|x'|\leq g(k)$ for some functions $f$ and $g$. The function $g(k)$ is called the {\em size} of the bikernel.
nodes.statement_short: A polynomial-time reduction between parameterized problems whose output size and parameter are bounded by functions of $k$ alone.
differentia: maps an instance $(x,k)$ to an instance $(x',k')$
(i)~$(x,k)\in L$ if and only if $(x',k')\in L'$

nodes.name: FPT characterization via bikernelization
nodes.statement: a parameterized problem $L$ is fixed-parameter tractable if and only if it is decidable and admits a bikernelization from itself to a parameterized problem $L'$.
assumptions: a parameterized problem $L$
conclusions: is fixed-parameter tractable if and only if it is decidable and admits a bikernelization from itself to a parameterized problem $L'$

nodes.name: Kernelization, kernel and its size
nodes.statement: A {\em kernelization} of a parameterized problem $L$ is simply a bikernelization from $L$ to itself; the bikernel is the {\em kernel}, and $g(k)$ is the {\em size} of the kernel.
differentia: $g(k)$ is the {\em size} of the kernel

nodes.name: Reducing several parameters to one
nodes.statement: The case of several parameters $k_1,\ldots ,k_t$ can be reduced to the one parameter case by setting $k=k_1+\cdots +k_t,$ see, e.g., \cite{DLS09}.

nodes.name: Yes-instances of MaxLin2-AA in terms of maximum excess
nodes.section: 2 Maximum Excess, Irreducible Systems and Algorithm $\cal H$
nodes.statement: Observe that the answer to {\sc MaxLin2-AA} is {\sc Yes} if and only if the maximum excess is at least $2k$.

nodes.name: Equivalence of maximum excess and maxima of pseudo-boolean functions
nodes.section: 2 Maximum Excess, Irreducible Systems and Algorithm $\cal H$
nodes.statement: The excess $\varepsilon_S(x)$ is a pseudo-boolean function and its Fourier expression is  $\varepsilon_S(x)=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\prod_{i\in I_j}x_i$. Moreover, observe that every pseudo-boolean function $f(x)=\sum_{I\in {\cal F}}\hat{f}(I)\prod_{i\in I}x_i$ (where $\hat{f}(\emptyset)=0$) is the excess over the system $\prod_{i\in I}x_i=b_I$, $I\in {\cal F}$, where $b_I=1$ if $\hat{f}(I)>0$ and $b_I=-1$ if $\hat{f}(I)<0$, with weights $|\hat{f}(I)|.$ Thus, studying the maximum excess over a {\sc MaxLin2-AA}-system (with real weights) is equivalent to studying the maximum of a pseudo-boolean function.
nodes.statement_short: Maximizing the excess of a {\sc MaxLin2-AA} system with real weights is the same problem as maximizing a pseudo-boolean function.

nodes.name: Reduction Rule 1
nodes.section: 2 Maximum Excess, Irreducible Systems and Algorithm $\cal H$
nodes.statement: If we have, for a subset $I$ of $[n]$, an equation $\prod_{i \in I} x_i =b_I'$ with weight $w_I'$, and an equation $\prod_{i \in I} x_i =b_I''$ with weight $w_I''$, then we replace this pair by one of these equations with weight $w_I'+w_I''$ if $b_I'=b_I''$ and, otherwise, by the equation whose weight is bigger, modifying its new weight to be the difference of the two old ones. If the resulting weight is~0, we delete the equation from the system.
nodes.statement_short: Merge two equations with the same left-hand side, adding weights if the right-hand sides agree and subtracting otherwise.
input: an equation $\prod_{i \in I} x_i =b_I'$ with weight $w_I'$
an equation $\prod_{i \in I} x_i =b_I''$ with weight $w_I''$
output: one of these equations with weight $w_I'+w_I''$ if $b_I'=b_I''$
the equation whose weight is bigger, modifying its new weight to be the difference of the two old ones

nodes.name: Reduction Rule 2
nodes.section: 2 Maximum Excess, Irreducible Systems and Algorithm $\cal H$
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be the matrix over $\mathbb{F}_2$ corresponding to the set of equations in $S$, such that $a_{ji} = 1$ if $i \in I_j$ and $0$, otherwise. Let $t={\rm rank} A$ and suppose columns $a^{i_1},\ldots ,a^{i_t}$ of $A$ are linearly independent. Then delete all variables not in $\{x_{i_1},\ldots ,x_{i_t}\}$ from the equations of $S$.
nodes.statement_short: Keep only variables indexing a maximal set of linearly independent columns of the $\mathbb{F}_2$-matrix of $S$.
input: the matrix over $\mathbb{F}_2$ corresponding to the set of equations in $S$, such that $a_{ji} = 1$ if $i \in I_j$ and $0$, otherwise
output: delete all variables not in $\{x_{i_1},\ldots ,x_{i_t}\}$ from the equations of $S$

nodes.name: Form the $\mathbb{F}_2$-matrix and pick independent columns
nodes.section: 2 Maximum Excess, Irreducible Systems and Algorithm $\cal H$
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be the matrix over $\mathbb{F}_2$ corresponding to the set of equations in $S$, such that $a_{ji} = 1$ if $i \in I_j$ and $0$, otherwise. Let $t={\rm rank} A$ and suppose columns $a^{i_1},\ldots ,a^{i_t}$ of $A$ are linearly independent.
nodes.statement_short: Build $A$ over $\mathbb{F}_2$ and select $t={\rm rank}A$ linearly independent columns.

nodes.name: Delete the redundant variables
nodes.section: 2 Maximum Excess, Irreducible Systems and Algorithm $\cal H$
nodes.statement: Then delete all variables not in $\{x_{i_1},\ldots ,x_{i_t}\}$ from the equations of $S$.
nodes.statement_short: Remove every variable outside the chosen independent set.

nodes.name: Reduction rules preserve the maximum excess
nodes.section: 2 Maximum Excess, Irreducible Systems and Algorithm $\cal H$
nodes.statement: \cite{GutKimSzeYeo11} Let $S'$ be obtained from $S$ by Rule~\ref{rule1} or \ref{rulerank}. Then the maximum excess of $S'$  is equal to the maximum excess of $S$. Moreover, $S'$ can be obtained from $S$ in time polynomial in $n$ and $m$.
assumptions: Let $S'$ be obtained from $S$ by Rule~\ref{rule1} or \ref{rulerank}
conclusions: the maximum excess of $S'$  is equal to the maximum excess of $S$
$S'$ can be obtained from $S$ in time polynomial in $n$ and $m$

nodes.name: Irreducible system
nodes.section: 2 Maximum Excess, Irreducible Systems and Algorithm $\cal H$
nodes.statement: If we cannot change a weighted system $S$ using  Rules~\ref{rule1} and \ref{rulerank}, we call it {\em irreducible}.
differentia: we cannot change a weighted system $S$ using  Rules~\ref{rule1} and \ref{rulerank}

nodes.name: Applying Rule 1 then Rule 2 yields an irreducible system
nodes.section: 2 Maximum Excess, Irreducible Systems and Algorithm $\cal H$
nodes.statement: Let $S'$ be a system obtained from $S$ by first applying Rule~\ref{rule1} as long as possible and then Rule \ref{rulerank} as long as possible. Then $S'$ is irreducible.
assumptions: Let $S'$ be a system obtained from $S$ by first applying Rule~\ref{rule1} as long as possible and then Rule \ref{rulerank} as long as possible
conclusions: $S'$ is irreducible

nodes.name: Proof that Rule 1 followed by Rule 2 gives an irreducible system
nodes.section: 2 Maximum Excess, Irreducible Systems and Algorithm $\cal H$
nodes.statement: Let $S^*$ denote the system obtained from $S$ by applying Rule~\ref{rule1} as long as possible. Without loss of generality, assume that $x_1\not\in \{x_{i_1},\ldots ,x_{i_t}\}$ (see the description of Rule \ref{rulerank}) and thus Rule \ref{rulerank} removes $x_1$ from $S^*$. To prove the lemma it suffices to show that after $x_1$ removal no pair of equations has the same left hand side. Suppose that there is a pair of equations in $S^*$ which has the same left hand side after $x_1$ removal; let $\prod_{i \in I'} x_i =b'$ and $\prod_{i \in I''} x_i =b''$ be such equations and let $I'=I''\cup \{1\}$. Then the entries of the first column of $A$, $a^1$, corresponding to the pair of equations are 1 and 0, but in all the other columns of $A$ the entries corresponding to the the pair of equations are either 1,1 or 0,0. Thus, $a^1$ is independent from all the other columns of $A$, a contradiction.\qed
nodes.statement_short: By contradiction: a repeated left-hand side after deleting $x_1$ would make the column $a^1$ independent of the rest.

nodes.name: Set up $S^*$ and the removed variable $x_1$
nodes.section: 2 Maximum Excess, Irreducible Systems and Algorithm $\cal H$
nodes.statement: Let $S^*$ denote the system obtained from $S$ by applying Rule~\ref{rule1} as long as possible. Without loss of generality, assume that $x_1\not\in \{x_{i_1},\ldots ,x_{i_t}\}$ (see the description of Rule \ref{rulerank}) and thus Rule \ref{rulerank} removes $x_1$ from $S^*$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix $S^*$ after Rule 1 and assume w.l.o.g. that Rule 2 deletes $x_1$.

nodes.name: Reduce the lemma to a statement about left-hand sides
nodes.section: 2 Maximum Excess, Irreducible Systems and Algorithm $\cal H$
nodes.statement: To prove the lemma it suffices to show that after $x_1$ removal no pair of equations has the same left hand side.
nodes.statement_short: It suffices to rule out duplicate left-hand sides after the deletion.

nodes.name: Derive a contradiction from a duplicate left-hand side
nodes.section: 2 Maximum Excess, Irreducible Systems and Algorithm $\cal H$
nodes.statement: Suppose that there is a pair of equations in $S^*$ which has the same left hand side after $x_1$ removal; let $\prod_{i \in I'} x_i =b'$ and $\prod_{i \in I''} x_i =b''$ be such equations and let $I'=I''\cup \{1\}$. Then the entries of the first column of $A$, $a^1$, corresponding to the pair of equations are 1 and 0, but in all the other columns of $A$ the entries corresponding to the the pair of equations are either 1,1 or 0,0. Thus, $a^1$ is independent from all the other columns of $A$, a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Such a pair forces $a^1$ to be independent of the other columns, contradicting the choice of Rule 2.

nodes.name: Algorithm $\cal H$
nodes.section: 2 Maximum Excess, Irreducible Systems and Algorithm $\cal H$
nodes.statement: \textsc{Algorithm $\cal H$} \smallskip While the system $S$ is nonempty and the total weight of marked equations is less than $2k$ do the following: \begin{enumerate} \item Choose an arbitrary equation  $\prod_{i \in I} x_i =b$ and mark an arbitrary variable $x_l$ such that $l \in I$. \item Mark this equation and delete it from the system. \item Replace every equation $\prod_{i \in I'} x_i =b'$ in the system containing $x_l$ by $\prod_{i \in I\Delta I'} x_i = bb'$, where $I\Delta I'$ is the symmetric difference of $I$ and $I'$ (the weight of the equation is unchanged). \item Apply Reduction Rule \ref{rule1} to the system. \end{enumerate} \smallskip
nodes.statement_short: Greedily mark equations and a variable of each, eliminate the marked variable by symmetric difference, and re-apply Rule 1, until marked weight reaches $2k$.
input: Let $S$ be an irreducible system of {\sc MaxLin2-AA}.
We assume that, in the beginning, no equation or variable in $S$ is marked.
output: the total weight of marked equations
an \emph{equivalent} system under the assumption that the marked equations are satisfied

nodes.name: Choose an equation and mark a variable
nodes.section: 2 Maximum Excess, Irreducible Systems and Algorithm $\cal H$
nodes.statement: Choose an arbitrary equation  $\prod_{i \in I} x_i =b$ and mark an arbitrary variable $x_l$ such that $l \in I$.
nodes.statement_short: Pick any equation and mark one of its variables $x_l$.

nodes.name: Mark and delete the chosen equation
nodes.section: 2 Maximum Excess, Irreducible Systems and Algorithm $\cal H$
nodes.statement: Mark this equation and delete it from the system.
nodes.statement_short: Mark it, then delete it.

nodes.name: Eliminate $x_l$ by symmetric difference
nodes.section: 2 Maximum Excess, Irreducible Systems and Algorithm $\cal H$
nodes.statement: Replace every equation $\prod_{i \in I'} x_i =b'$ in the system containing $x_l$ by $\prod_{i \in I\Delta I'} x_i = bb'$, where $I\Delta I'$ is the symmetric difference of $I$ and $I'$ (the weight of the equation is unchanged).
nodes.statement_short: Add the marked equation to every equation containing $x_l$, keeping weights.

nodes.name: Re-apply Reduction Rule 1
nodes.section: 2 Maximum Excess, Irreducible Systems and Algorithm $\cal H$
nodes.statement: Apply Reduction Rule \ref{rule1} to the system.
nodes.statement_short: Re-apply Rule 1.

nodes.name: Algorithm $\cal H$ produces an equivalent system
nodes.section: 2 Maximum Excess, Irreducible Systems and Algorithm $\cal H$
nodes.statement: Note that algorithm ${\cal H}$ replaces $S$ with an \emph{equivalent} system under the assumption that the marked equations are satisfied; that is, for every assignment of values to the variables $x_1, \ldots, x_n$ that satisfies the marked equations, both systems have the same excess.
nodes.statement_short: Conditioned on the marked equations being satisfied, $\cal H$ preserves the excess of every assignment.

nodes.name: Marked weight lower-bounds the maximum excess
nodes.section: 2 Maximum Excess, Irreducible Systems and Algorithm $\cal H$
nodes.statement: \cite{CroGutJonKimRuz10} Let $S$ be an irreducible system and assume that Algorithm $\cal H$ marks equations of total weight $w$. Then the maximum excess of $S$ is at least $w$. In particular, if $w\ge 2k$ then $S$ is a {\sc Yes}-instance of {\sc MaxLin2-AA}[$k$].
assumptions: Let $S$ be an irreducible system
assume that Algorithm $\cal H$ marks equations of total weight $w$
conclusions: the maximum excess of $S$ is at least $w$
if $w\ge 2k$ then $S$ is a {\sc Yes}-instance of {\sc MaxLin2-AA}[$k$]

nodes.name: $n^{2k}(nm)^{O(1)}$-time algorithm for MaxLin2-AA[$k$]
nodes.statement: There exists an $n^{2k}(nm)^{O(1)}$-time algorithm for {\sc MaxLin2-AA}[$k$] that returns an assignment of excess of at least $2k$ if one exists, and returns {\sc no} otherwise.
assumptions: for {\sc MaxLin2-AA}[$k$]
conclusions: There exists an $n^{2k}(nm)^{O(1)}$-time algorithm for {\sc MaxLin2-AA}[$k$] that returns an assignment of excess of at least $2k$ if one exists, and returns {\sc no} otherwise

nodes.name: Proof of the $n^{2k}(nm)^{O(1)}$-time algorithm
nodes.statement: Suppose we have an instance $\cal L$ of {\sc MaxLin2-AA}[$k$] that is reduced by Rules \ref{rule1} and \ref{rulerank}, and that the maximum excess of $\cal L$ is at least $2k$. Let $A$ be the matrix introduced in Rule \ref{rulerank}. Pick $n$ equations $e_1,\ldots , e_n$ such that their rows in $A$ are linearly independent. Any assignment must either satisfy one of these equations, or falsify them all. We can check, in time $(nm)^{O(1)}$, what happens if they are all falsified, as fixing the values of these $n$ equations fixes the values of all the others. If falsifying all the equations does not lead to an excess of at least $2k$, then any assignment of values to $x_1,\ldots ,x_n$ that leads to excess at least $2k$ must satisfy at least one of $e_1, \ldots ,e_n$. Thus, by Lemma \ref{lemExcess}, algorithm $\cal H$ can mark one of these equations and achieve an excess of at least $2k$. This gives us the following depth-bounded search tree. At each node $N$ of the tree, reduce the system by Rules  \ref{rule1} and \ref{rulerank}, and let $n'$ be the number of variables in the reduced system. Then find $n'$ equations $e_1,\ldots ,e_{n'}$ corresponding to linearly independent vectors. Find an assignment of values to $x_1,\ldots ,x_{n'}$ that falsifies all of $e_1,\ldots , e_{n'}$. Check whether this assignment achieves excess of at least $2k-w^*$, where $w^*$ is total weight of equations marked by $\cal H$ in all predecessors of $N$. If it does, then return the assignment and stop the algorithm. Otherwise, split into $n'$ branches. In the $i$'th branch, run an iteration of $\cal H$ marking equation $e_i$. Then repeat this algorithm for each new node. Whenever the total weight of marked equations is at least $2k,$ return the suitable assignment. Clearly, the algorithm will terminate without an assignment if the maximum excess of $\cal L$ is less than $2k.$ All the operations at each node take time $(nm)^{O(1)}$, and there are less than $n^{2k+1}$ nodes in the search tree. Therefore this algorithm takes time $n^{2k}(nm)^{O(1)}$.\qed
nodes.statement_short: Branch on which of $n'$ linearly independent equations Algorithm $\cal H$ marks, giving a depth-bounded search tree with $<n^{2k+1}$ nodes.

nodes.name: Any excess-$2k$ assignment satisfies one independent equation
nodes.statement: Suppose we have an instance $\cal L$ of {\sc MaxLin2-AA}[$k$] that is reduced by Rules \ref{rule1} and \ref{rulerank}, and that the maximum excess of $\cal L$ is at least $2k$. Let $A$ be the matrix introduced in Rule \ref{rulerank}. Pick $n$ equations $e_1,\ldots , e_n$ such that their rows in $A$ are linearly independent. Any assignment must either satisfy one of these equations, or falsify them all. We can check, in time $(nm)^{O(1)}$, what happens if they are all falsified, as fixing the values of these $n$ equations fixes the values of all the others. If falsifying all the equations does not lead to an excess of at least $2k$, then any assignment of values to $x_1,\ldots ,x_n$ that leads to excess at least $2k$ must satisfy at least one of $e_1, \ldots ,e_n$. Thus, by Lemma \ref{lemExcess}, algorithm $\cal H$ can mark one of these equations and achieve an excess of at least $2k$.
nodes.statement_short: Either all $n$ independent equations are falsified (checkable directly) or one is satisfied and can be marked by $\cal H$.

nodes.name: Build the depth-bounded search tree
nodes.statement: This gives us the following depth-bounded search tree. At each node $N$ of the tree, reduce the system by Rules  \ref{rule1} and \ref{rulerank}, and let $n'$ be the number of variables in the reduced system. Then find $n'$ equations $e_1,\ldots ,e_{n'}$ corresponding to linearly independent vectors. Find an assignment of values to $x_1,\ldots ,x_{n'}$ that falsifies all of $e_1,\ldots , e_{n'}$. Check whether this assignment achieves excess of at least $2k-w^*$, where $w^*$ is total weight of equations marked by $\cal H$ in all predecessors of $N$. If it does, then return the assignment and stop the algorithm. Otherwise, split into $n'$ branches. In the $i$'th branch, run an iteration of $\cal H$ marking equation $e_i$. Then repeat this algorithm for each new node. Whenever the total weight of marked equations is at least $2k,$ return the suitable assignment. Clearly, the algorithm will terminate without an assignment if the maximum excess of $\cal L$ is less than $2k.$
nodes.statement_short: Branch into $n'$ subcases at each node, running one iteration of $\cal H$ per branch.

nodes.name: Bound the running time
nodes.statement: All the operations at each node take time $(nm)^{O(1)}$, and there are less than $n^{2k+1}$ nodes in the search tree. Therefore this algorithm takes time $n^{2k}(nm)^{O(1)}$.
nodes.statement_short: $<n^{2k+1}$ nodes times $(nm)^{O(1)}$ work each gives $n^{2k}(nm)^{O(1)}$.

nodes.name: Proof of the $O(k^2\log k)$-variable kernel
nodes.statement: Let $\cal L$ be an instance of {\sc MaxLin2-AA}[$k$] and let $S$ be the system of $\cal L$ with $m$ equations and $n$ variables. We may assume that $S$ is irreducible. Let the parameter $k$ be an arbitrary positive integer. If $m<2k$ then $n<2k=O(k^2\log k)$. If $2k\le m\le 2^{n/(2k-1)}-2$ then, by Theorem \ref{thm:ing2}, the answer to $\cal L$ is {\sc yes} and the corresponding assignment can be found in polynomial time. If $m\ge n^{2k}$ then, by Theorem \ref{thm:ing1}, we can solve $\cal L$ in polynomial time. Finally we consider the case $2^{n/(2k-1)}-1 \le m \le n^{2k}-1$. Hence, $n^{2k}\ge 2^{n/(2k-1)}.$ Therefore, $4k^2\ge 2+n/\log n \ge \sqrt{n}$ and $n\le (2k)^4$. Hence, $n\le 4k^2\log n\le 4k^2\log(16k^4)=O(k^2\log k).$ Since $S$ is irreducible, $m<2^n$ and thus we have obtained the desired kernel. \qed

nodes.statement: Let $K$ and $M$ be sets of vectors in $\mathbb{F}^n_2$ such that $K \subseteq M$. We say $K$ is \emph{$M$-sum-free} if no sum of two or more distinct vectors in $K$ is equal to a vector in $M$.

nodes.name: Proof of the $M$-sum-free subset lemma
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbf{1} = (1, \ldots, 1)$ be the vector in $\mathbb{F}^n_2$ in which every coordinate is $1$. Note that $\mathbf{1}\not\in M.$ By our assumption $M$ contains a basis of $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ and we may find such a basis in polynomial time (using Gaussian elimination, see above). We may write $\mathbf{1}$ as a sum of some vectors of this basis $B$. This implies that $\mathbf{1}$ can be expressed as follows: $\mathbf{1} = v_1 + v_2 + \cdots + v_s$, where $\{v_1, \ldots, v_s\}\subseteq B$ and $v_1, \ldots, v_s$ are linearly independent, and we can find such an expression in polynomial time. For each $v \in M \backslash \{v_1, \ldots, v_s\}$, consider the set $S_v=\{v, v_1, \ldots, v_s\}$. In polynomial time, we may check whether $S_v$ is linearly independent. Consider two cases: \begin{description} \item[Case 1:] $S_v$ is linearly independent for each $v \in M \backslash \{v_1, \ldots, v_s\}$. Then $\{v_1, \ldots, v_s\}$ is $M$-sum-free (here we also use the fact that $\{v_1, \ldots, v_s\}$ is linearly independent). Since each $v_i$ has at most $r$ positive coordinates, we have $sr\ge n> r(k-1)$. Hence, $s>k-1$ implying that $s\ge k$. Thus, $\{v_1, \ldots, v_k\}$ is the required set $K$. \item[Case 2:] $S_v$ is linearly dependent for some $v\in M \backslash \{v_1, \ldots, v_s\}$. Then we can find (in polynomial time) $I \subseteq [s]$ such that $v=\sum_{i \in I} v_i$. Thus, we have a shorter expression for $\mathbf{1}$: $\mathbf{1} = v'_1 + v'_2 + \cdots + v'_{s'}$, where $\{v'_1, \ldots , v'_{s'}\}=\{v\} \cup \{ v_i : i \notin I\}$. Note that $\{v'_1, \ldots , v'_{s'}\}$ is linearly independent. \end{description} Since $s\le n$ and Case 2 produces a shorter expression for $\mathbf{1}$, after at most $n$ iterations of Case 2 we will arrive at Case 1. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Iteratively shorten an expression of the all-ones vector over a basis until every extension stays independent; the resulting set is $M$-sum-free and has size $\ge k$.

nodes.name: Proof of the maximum-excess lower bound
nodes.statement: Consider a set $M$ of vectors in $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ corresponding to equations in $S$ as follows: for each equation $\prod_{i \in I} x_i =b$ in $S$, define a vector $v=(v_1,\ldots ,v_{n})\in M$, where $v_i=1$ if $i\in I$ and $v_i=0$, otherwise. As $S$ is reduced by Rule \ref{rulerank} we have that $M$ contains a basis for $\mathbb{F}^n_2$, and each vector contains at most $r$ non-zero coordinates and $n\ge (k-1)r+1$. Therefore, using Lemma \ref{thmKcon} we can find an $M$-sum-free set $K$ of $k$ vectors. Let $\{e_{j_1}, \ldots, e_{j_k}\}$ be the corresponding set of equations. Run Algorithm $\cal H$, choosing at Step 1 an equation of $S$ from $\{e_{j_1}, \ldots, e_{j_k}\}$ each time, and let $S'$ be the resulting system. Algorithm $\cal H$ will run for $k$ iterations of the while loop as no equation from $\{e_{j_1}, \ldots, e_{j_k}\}$ will be deleted before it has been marked. Indeed, suppose that this is not true. Then for some $e_{j_l}$ and some other equation $e$ in $S$, after applying Algorithm $\cal H$ for at most $l-1$ iterations $e_{j_l}$ and $e$ contain the same variables. Thus, there are vectors $v_j\in K$ and $v\in M$ and a pair of nonintersecting subsets $K'$ and $K''$ of $K\setminus \{v,v_j\}$ such that $v_j+\sum_{u\in K'}u=v+\sum_{u\in K''}u$. Thus, $v=v_j+\sum_{u\in K'\cup K''}u$, a contradiction with the definition of $K.$ Thus, by Lemma \ref{lemExcess}, we are done. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Feed an $M$-sum-free set of $k$ equations to Algorithm $\cal H$; sum-freeness prevents early deletion, so $k$ equations get marked.

nodes.name: Sharpness of the condition $n \ge r(k-1)+1$
nodes.statement: To see that the inequality $n \ge r(k-1)+1$ in the theorem is best possible assume that $n=r(k-1)$ and consider a partition of $[n]$ into $k-1$ subsets $N_1,\ldots ,N_{k-1}$, each of size $r.$ Let $S$ be the system consisting of subsystems $S_i$, $i\in [k-1],$ such that a subsystem $S_i$ is comprised of equations $\prod_{i \in I} x_i=-1$ of weight 1 for every $I$ such that $\emptyset \neq I\subseteq N_i$. Now assume without loss of generality that $N_i=[r]$. Observe that the assignment $(x_1,\ldots ,x_r)=(1,\ldots ,1)$ falsifies all equations of $S_i$ but by setting $x_j=-1$ for any $j\in [r]$ we satisfy the equation $x_j=-1$ and turn the remaining equations into pairs of the form $\prod_{i \in I} x_i=-1$ and $\prod_{i \in I} x_i=1$. Thus, the maximum excess of $S_i$ is 1 and the maximum excess of $S$ is $k-1$.
nodes.statement_short: For $n=r(k-1)$ a block construction has maximum excess only $k-1$, so the hypothesis cannot be weakened.

nodes.statement_short: With $W=O(n)$ the ratio $W/(2\lfloor(n+r-1)/r\rfloor)$ is $O(1)$.

nodes.name: Max-$r$-CSP
nodes.origin_citation: Alon, Gutin, Kim, Szeider \& Yeo 2011; Kim \& Williams 2010
nodes.statement: The (parameterized) Boolean Max-$r$-Constraint Satisfaction Problem ({\sc Max-$r$-CSP}) generalizes {\sc MaxLin2-AA}[$k,r$] as follows: We are given a set $\Phi$ of Boolean functions, each involving at most $r$ variables, and a collection ${\cal F}$ of $m$ Boolean functions, each $f \in \cal F$ being a member of $\Phi$, and each acting on some subset of the $n$ Boolean variables $x_1,x_2, \ldots ,x_n$ (each $x_i\in \{-1,1\}$). We are to decide whether there is a truth assignment to the $n$ variables such that the total number of satisfied functions is at least $E+k$, where  $E$ is the average value of the number of satisfied functions. The parameters are $k$ and $r$.
nodes.statement_short: Decide whether some assignment satisfies at least $E+k$ of $m$ $r$-ary Boolean constraints, where $E$ is the average.

nodes.name: Bikernel with $(k2^{r+1}-1)r$ variables for Max-$r$-CSP
nodes.statement: Using a bikernelization algorithm described in \cite{AloGutKimSzeYeo11,CroGutJonKimRuz10} and our new kernel result, it easy to see that {\sc Max-$r$-CSP} with parameters $k$ and $r$ admits a bikernel with at most $(k2^{r+1}-1)r$ variables. This result improves the corresponding result of Kim and Williams \cite{KimWil} ($n\le kr(r+1)2^r$).
nodes.statement_short: Combining known bikernelization with the new kernel gives a $(k2^{r+1}-1)r$-variable bikernel for {\sc Max-$r$-CSP}.
assumptions: Using a bikernelization algorithm described in \cite{AloGutKimSzeYeo11,CroGutJonKimRuz10} and our new kernel result
conclusions: {\sc Max-$r$-CSP} with parameters $k$ and $r$ admits a bikernel with at most $(k2^{r+1}-1)r$ variables

nodes.name: Lower bound on the maximum of a pseudo-boolean function of degree $r$
nodes.statement: Let \begin{equation} f(x)=\hat{f}(\emptyset) + \sum_{I\in {\cal F}}\hat{f}(I)\prod_{i\in I}x_i\end{equation} be a pseudo-boolean function of degree $r$. Then \begin{equation}\max_x f(x)\ge \hat{f}(\emptyset) + \lfloor ({\rm rank} A +r -1)/r\rfloor \cdot \min \{|\hat{f}(I)|: I\in {\cal F}\},\end{equation} where $A$ is a $(0,1)$-matrix with entries $a_{ij}$ such that $a_{ij}=1$ if and only if term $j$ in (\ref{fourier}) contains $x_i.$ One can find an assignment of values to $x$ satisfying (\ref{LBpb1t}) in time $(n|{\cal F}|)^{O(1)}.$
nodes.statement_short: The maximum of a degree-$r$ pseudo-boolean function exceeds its constant term by $\lfloor({\rm rank}A+r-1)/r\rfloor$ times the smallest $|\hat f(I)|$.
assumptions: Let \begin{equation} f(x)=\hat{f}(\emptyset) + \sum_{I\in {\cal F}}\hat{f}(I)\prod_{i\in I}x_i\end{equation} be a pseudo-boolean function of degree $r$
where $A$ is a $(0,1)$-matrix with entries $a_{ij}$ such that $a_{ij}=1$ if and only if term $j$ in (\ref{fourier}) contains $x_i.$
conclusions: \begin{equation}\max_x f(x)\ge \hat{f}(\emptyset) + \lfloor ({\rm rank} A +r -1)/r\rfloor \cdot \min \{|\hat{f}(I)|: I\in {\cal F}\},\end{equation}
One can find an assignment of values to $x$ satisfying (\ref{LBpb1t}) in time $(n|{\cal F}|)^{O(1)}.$

nodes.name: Proof of the pseudo-boolean lower bound
nodes.statement: By Remark \ref{PseudoBExcess} the function $f(x) - \hat{f}(\emptyset) =\sum_{I\in {\cal F}}\hat{f}(I)\prod_{i\in I}x_i$ is the excess over the system $\prod_{i\in I}x_i=b_I$, $I\in {\cal F}$, where $b_I=+1$ if $\hat{f}(I)>0$ and $b_I=-1$ if $\hat{f}(I)<0$, with weights $|\hat{f}(I)|.$ Clearly, Rule \ref{rule1} will not change the system. Using Rule \ref{rulerank} we can replace the system by an equivalent one (by Lemma \ref{lem:SS'}) with ${\rm rank} A$ variables. By Lemma \ref{lem:irred}, the new system is irreducible and we can now apply Theorem \ref{lemYes}. By this theorem, Remark \ref{PseudoBExcess} and Remark \ref{rem:reals}, $\max_x f(x)\ge  \hat{f}(\emptyset)+k^*\min \{|\hat{f}(I)|: I\in {\cal F}\}$, where $k^*$ is the maximum value of $k$ satisfying ${\rm rank} A\ge (k-1)r+1$. It remains to observe that $k^*=\lfloor ({\rm rank} A +r -1)/r\rfloor$. \qed
nodes.statement_short: View $f-\hat f(\emptyset)$ as an excess, reduce to ${\rm rank}A$ variables, and apply the excess bound with real weights.

nodes.name: Realize $f-\hat f(\emptyset)$ as an excess
nodes.statement: By Remark \ref{PseudoBExcess} the function $f(x) - \hat{f}(\emptyset) =\sum_{I\in {\cal F}}\hat{f}(I)\prod_{i\in I}x_i$ is the excess over the system $\prod_{i\in I}x_i=b_I$, $I\in {\cal F}$, where $b_I=+1$ if $\hat{f}(I)>0$ and $b_I=-1$ if $\hat{f}(I)<0$, with weights $|\hat{f}(I)|.$
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite $f-\hat f(\emptyset)$ as the excess of an explicit weighted system.

nodes.name: Reduce the system and check irreducibility
nodes.statement: Clearly, Rule \ref{rule1} will not change the system. Using Rule \ref{rulerank} we can replace the system by an equivalent one (by Lemma \ref{lem:SS'}) with ${\rm rank} A$ variables. By Lemma \ref{lem:irred}, the new system is irreducible and we can now apply Theorem \ref{lemYes}.
nodes.statement_short: Rule 2 shrinks the system to ${\rm rank}A$ variables and leaves it irreducible.

nodes.name: Apply the excess bound with parameter $k^*$
nodes.statement: By this theorem, Remark \ref{PseudoBExcess} and Remark \ref{rem:reals}, $\max_x f(x)\ge  \hat{f}(\emptyset)+k^*\min \{|\hat{f}(I)|: I\in {\cal F}\}$, where $k^*$ is the maximum value of $k$ satisfying ${\rm rank} A\ge (k-1)r+1$.
nodes.statement_short: The real-weight excess bound gives the inequality with the largest admissible $k^*$.

nodes.name: Evaluate $k^*$
nodes.statement: It remains to observe that $k^*=\lfloor ({\rm rank} A +r -1)/r\rfloor$.
nodes.statement_short: Compute $k^*=\lfloor({\rm rank}A+r-1)/r\rfloor$.

nodes.name: Incidence matrix of a graph
nodes.statement: For a graph $G=(V,E)$, an incidence matrix is a $(0,1)$-matrix with entries $m_{e,v}$, $e\in E$, $v\in V$ such that $m_{e,v}=1$ if and only if $v$ is incident to $e$.
differentia: $m_{e,v}=1$ if and only if $v$ is incident to $e$

nodes.name: Rank of the incidence matrix of a connected graph
nodes.statement: The rank of an incident matrix $M$ of a connected graph equals $|V|-1.$
assumptions: an incident matrix $M$ of a connected graph
conclusions: The rank of an incident matrix $M$ of a connected graph equals $|V|-1.$

nodes.name: Edwards-Erd{\H o}s bound
nodes.statement: Let $G=(V,E)$ be a connected graph with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges. Then $G$ contains a bipartite subgraph with at least $\frac{m}{2} + \frac{n-1}{4}$ edges. Such a subgraph can be found in polynomial time.
nodes.statement_short: Every connected graph has a bipartite subgraph with at least $m/2+(n-1)/4$ edges, constructible in polynomial time.
assumptions: Let $G=(V,E)$ be a connected graph with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges
conclusions: $G$ contains a bipartite subgraph with at least $\frac{m}{2} + \frac{n-1}{4}$ edges
Such a subgraph can be found in polynomial time

nodes.name: New proof of the Edwards-Erd{\H o}s bound
nodes.statement: Let $V=\{v_1,v_2,\ldots , v_n\}$ and let $c:\ V\rightarrow \{-1,1\}$ be a 2-coloring of $G$. Observe that the maximum number of edges in a bipartite subgraph of $G$ equals the maximum number of properly colored edges (i.e., edges whose end-vertices received different colors) over all 2-colorings of $G$. For an edge $e=v_iv_j\in E$ consider the following function $f_e(x)=\frac{1}{2}(1-x_ix_j)$, where $x_i=c(v_i)$ and $x_j=c(v_j)$ and observe that $f_e(x)=1$ if $e$ is properly colored by $c$ and $f_e(x)=0,$ otherwise. Thus, $f(x)=\sum_{e\in E}f_e(x)$ is the number of properly colored edges for $c$. We have $f(x)=\frac{m}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{e\in E}x_ix_j$. By Theorem \ref{thm:PBB}, $\max_x f(x)\ge m/2 + \lfloor ({\rm rank} A +2 -1)/2\rfloor/2.$ Observe that matrix $A$ in this bound is  an incidence matrix of $G$ and, thus, by Lemma \ref{lem:M} ${\rm rank} A = n-1$. Hence, $\max_x f(x)\ge \frac{m}{2} + \frac{1}{2}\lfloor \frac{n}{2} \rfloor \ge \frac{m}{2} + \frac{n-1}{4}$ as required. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Encode proper colorings as a degree-2 pseudo-boolean function and apply the Fourier lower bound with ${\rm rank}A=n-1$.

nodes.name: Restate Max Cut via 2-colorings
nodes.statement: Let $V=\{v_1,v_2,\ldots , v_n\}$ and let $c:\ V\rightarrow \{-1,1\}$ be a 2-coloring of $G$. Observe that the maximum number of edges in a bipartite subgraph of $G$ equals the maximum number of properly colored edges (i.e., edges whose end-vertices received different colors) over all 2-colorings of $G$.
nodes.statement_short: Largest bipartite subgraph = most properly colored edges over 2-colorings.

nodes.name: Build the degree-2 pseudo-boolean function
nodes.statement: For an edge $e=v_iv_j\in E$ consider the following function $f_e(x)=\frac{1}{2}(1-x_ix_j)$, where $x_i=c(v_i)$ and $x_j=c(v_j)$ and observe that $f_e(x)=1$ if $e$ is properly colored by $c$ and $f_e(x)=0,$ otherwise. Thus, $f(x)=\sum_{e\in E}f_e(x)$ is the number of properly colored edges for $c$. We have $f(x)=\frac{m}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{e\in E}x_ix_j$.
nodes.statement_short: Set $f(x)=\frac{m}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{e}x_ix_j$, counting properly colored edges.

nodes.name: Apply the pseudo-boolean lower bound
nodes.statement: By Theorem \ref{thm:PBB}, $\max_x f(x)\ge m/2 + \lfloor ({\rm rank} A +2 -1)/2\rfloor/2.$
nodes.statement_short: The degree-2 bound gives $\max_x f\ge m/2+\lfloor({\rm rank}A+1)/2\rfloor/2$.

nodes.name: Identify $A$ as the incidence matrix and conclude
nodes.statement: Observe that matrix $A$ in this bound is  an incidence matrix of $G$ and, thus, by Lemma \ref{lem:M} ${\rm rank} A = n-1$. Hence, $\max_x f(x)\ge \frac{m}{2} + \frac{1}{2}\lfloor \frac{n}{2} \rfloor \ge \frac{m}{2} + \frac{n-1}{4}$ as required.
nodes.statement_short: With ${\rm rank}A=n-1$ the bound becomes $m/2+(n-1)/4$.

nodes.name: Balance Subgraph
nodes.statement: This theorem can be extended to the {\sc Balance Subgraph} problem \cite{BocHufTruWah2009}, where we are given a graph $G=(V,E)$ in which each edge is labeled either by $=$ or by $\neq$ and we are asked to find a 2-coloring of $V$ such that the maximum number of edges is satisfied; an edge labeled by $=$ ($\neq$, resp.) is {\em satisfied} if and only if the colors of its end-vertices are the same (different, resp.).
nodes.statement_short: Find a 2-coloring maximizing the number of satisfied $=$/$\neq$-labeled edges.

nodes.name: Edwards-Erd{\H o}s-type bound for Balance Subgraph
nodes.statement: Let $G=(V,E)$ be a connected graph with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges labeled by either $=$ or $\neq$. There is a 2-coloring of $V$ that satisfies at least $\frac{m}{2} + \frac{n-1}{4}$ edges of $G$. Such a 2-coloring can be found in polynomial time.
nodes.statement_short: The $m/2+(n-1)/4$ bound extends from Max Cut to labeled ($=$/$\neq$) edges.
assumptions: Let $G=(V,E)$ be a connected graph with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges labeled by either $=$ or $\neq$
conclusions: There is a 2-coloring of $V$ that satisfies at least $\frac{m}{2} + \frac{n-1}{4}$ edges of $G$
Such a 2-coloring can be found in polynomial time

nodes.name: Proof of the Balance Subgraph bound
nodes.statement: Let $V=\{v_1,v_2,\ldots , v_n\}$ and let $c:\ V\rightarrow \{-1,1\}$ be a 2-coloring of $G$. Let $x_p=c(v_p)$, $p\in [n].$ For an edge $v_iv_j\in E$ we set $s_{ij}=1$ if $v_iv_j$ is labeled by $\neq$ and $s_{ij}=-1$ if $v_iv_j$ is labeled by $=$. Then the function $\frac{1}{2}\sum_{v_iv_j\in E}(1-s_{ij}x_ix_j)$ counts the number of edges satisfied by $c$. The rest of the proof is similar to that in the previous theorem. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Same argument as for Max Cut with signs $s_{ij}$ encoding the edge labels.

nodes.name: Fix a 2-coloring and its variables
nodes.statement: Let $V=\{v_1,v_2,\ldots , v_n\}$ and let $c:\ V\rightarrow \{-1,1\}$ be a 2-coloring of $G$. Let $x_p=c(v_p)$, $p\in [n].$
nodes.statement_short: Encode a 2-coloring as $\pm 1$ variables $x_p$.

nodes.name: Introduce edge signs and the counting function
nodes.statement: For an edge $v_iv_j\in E$ we set $s_{ij}=1$ if $v_iv_j$ is labeled by $\neq$ and $s_{ij}=-1$ if $v_iv_j$ is labeled by $=$. Then the function $\frac{1}{2}\sum_{v_iv_j\in E}(1-s_{ij}x_ix_j)$ counts the number of edges satisfied by $c$.
nodes.statement_short: Signs $s_{ij}$ turn satisfied-edge counting into a degree-2 pseudo-boolean function.

nodes.name: Repeat the previous argument
nodes.statement: The rest of the proof is similar to that in the previous theorem.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude exactly as in the Max Cut proof.

nodes.name: Parameterized complexity of Max Cut above the Edwards-Erd{\H o}s bound
nodes.statement: Another question of Mahajan et al. \cite{MahajanRamanSikdar09} remains open: what is the parameterized complexity of deciding whether a connected graph on $n$ vertices and $m$ edges has a bipartite subgraph with at least $m/2+(n-1)/4 + k$ edges, where $k$ is the parameter. Fixed-parameter tractability of a weaker problem was proved by Bollob{\'a}s and Scott \cite{BolSco2002} a decade ago.
nodes.statement_short: Is Max Cut parameterized above $m/2+(n-1)/4$ fixed-parameter tractable?

nodes.name: Polynomial-size kernel for MaxLin2-AA[$k$]
nodes.statement: The kernel obtained in Theorem \ref{thm:main} is not of polynomial size as it is not polynomial in $m$. The existence of a polynomial-size kernel for \textsc{MaxLin2-AA}[$k$] remains an open problem.
nodes.statement_short: Does {\sc MaxLin2-AA}[$k$] admit a kernel of polynomial size (not just polynomially many variables)?

nodes.name: Structural characterization of irreducible systems of small maximum excess
nodes.statement: Perhaps the kernel obtained in Theorem \ref{thm:main} or the algorithm of Corollary \ref{cor1} can be improved if we find a structural characterization of irreducible systems for which the maximum excess is less than $2k.$ Such a characterization can be of interest by itself.
nodes.statement_short: Characterize structurally the irreducible systems whose maximum excess is below $2k$.

nodes.name: MaxSat-AA[$k$] and Max-$r$-Sat-AA[$k$]
nodes.statement: Let $F$ be a CNF formula with clauses $C_1,\ldots ,C_m$ of sizes $r_1,\ldots ,r_m$. Since the probability of $C_i$ being satisfied by a random assignment is $1-2^{-r_i}$, the expected (average) number of satisfied clauses is $E=\sum_{i=1}^m(1-2^{-r_i}).$ It is natural to consider the following parameterized problem {\sc MaxSat-AA}[$k$]: decide whether there is a truth assignment that satisfies at least $E+k$ clauses. When there is a constant $r$ such that $|C_i|\le r$ for each $i=1,\ldots ,m$, {\sc MaxSat-AA}[$k$] is denoted by {\sc Max-$r$-Sat-AA}[$k$].
nodes.statement_short: Decide whether a CNF formula has an assignment satisfying at least $E+k$ clauses, where $E=\sum_i(1-2^{-r_i})$.

nodes.name: Fixed-parameter tractability of Max-$r$-Sat-AA[$k$]
nodes.statement: Mahajan et al. \cite{MahajanRamanSikdar09} asked what is the complexity of {\sc Max-$r$-Sat-AA}[$k$] and Alon et al. \cite{AloGutKimSzeYeo11} proved that it is fixed-parameter tractable \cite{AloGutKimSzeYeo11}.
nodes.statement_short: {\sc Max-$r$-Sat-AA}[$k$] is fixed-parameter tractable.
assumptions: {\sc Max-$r$-Sat-AA}[$k$]
conclusions: it is fixed-parameter tractable

nodes.name: Complexity of MaxSat-AA[$k$]
nodes.statement: It would be interesting to determine the complexity of {\sc MaxSat-AA}[$k$].
